notes.text: The burden — The prophet seems to speak of these grievous things, as a burden which he himself groaned under.

Therefore — Because the wicked go on with impunity. The law - The whole law, moral, ceremonial, and judicial. Is slacked - Is slighted, and not observed. Go forth - From magistrates, Judges, and public officers. Doth compass about - As it were besieges, with design to oppress and ruin.
Pure — Without the least mixture of falsehood.
Everlasting — The same in all ages and places.
Trouble — Outward troubles and anguish of spirit.
Congratulates their constancy in the faith, and exhorts them to advance daily in grace and wisdom.
Reforms their mistake concerning the coming of our Lord And,

Recommends several Christian duties. The parts of it are five: I. The inscription, Chap. i. 1, 2 II. Thanksgiving and prayer for them, 3-12 III. The doctrine concerning the man of sin,. ii. 1-12 Whence he comforts them against this trial, 13, 14 Adding exhortation and prayer, 15-17 IV. An exhortation to prayer, with a prayer for. iii. 1-5 them, to correct the disorderly, 6-16 V. The conclusion, 17, 18 2nd THESSALONIANS
Which ye endure — "That ye may be accounted worthy of the kingdom."

glossa.text: *To give thanks,* etc. Here he gives thanks to God for their good things, lest perchance they be lifted up over so great a good as they had from God, as though they had it from themselves. *Toward one another.* Namely, that he who is loved may love others, and by mutual services show forth charity.

notes.text: He passed through Jericho — So that Zacchaeus must have lived near the end of the town: the tree was in the town itself. And he was rich - These words seem to refer to the discourse in the last chapter, ver. 24, particularly to ver. 27. Zacchiaeus is a proof, that it is possible by the power of God for even a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven.
The chief of the publicans — What we would term, commissioner of the customs. A very honourable as well as profitable place.
And running before — With great earnestness. He climbed up - Notwithstanding his quality: desire conquering honour and shame.
Jesus said, Zacchaeus, make haste and come down — What a strange mixture of passions must Zacchaeus have now felt, hearing one speak, as knowing both his name and his heart!
They all murmured — All who were near: though most of them rather out of surprise than indignation.
And Zacchaeus stood — Showing by his posture, his deliberate, purpose and ready mind, and said, Behold, Lord, I give - I determine to do it immediately.
He also is a son of Abraham — A Jew born, and as such has a right to the first offer of salvation.
Matt. xviii, 11.

glossa.text:
*And entering in,* etc. Behold, the camel, having laid down the burden of its hump, passes through the eye of the needle, while, despising the revenue got by frauds, it climbs up to the narrow gate which leads to life. And because by the devotion of faith he supplies, by the climbing of a tree, what he had too little of by nature for seeing the Saviour, justly he receives what he did not dare to ask, the blessing of the Lord's welcome which he had desired. Mystically, Zacchaeus, who is interpreted *justified,* signifies those believing from among the Gentiles, who had been pressed down by the business of temporal things, and were least, but were sanctified by the Lord.

*And he was rich.* Who should despair of himself, when this man came to God whose revenue was from fraud? By him it appears that not every rich man is covetous.

*Because of the crowd.* What crowd, but the confusion of an unskilled multitude, which cannot see the summit of wisdom? Zacchaeus therefore, not in the crowd, but having passed beyond the common people, beholds the Messiah whom he desires.

*A sycomore.* The sycomore is a tree, like the mulberry in its leaves, but surpassing it in height, and it is interpreted *the foolish fig,* that is, the cross. Which, as a fig, feeds believers; as foolish, is mocked by unbelievers. The little man climbs it when anyone humble and conscious of his own weakness glories in the virtue of the cross, and through this praiseworthy foolishness discerns the Lord passing near; because if not yet so solidly as he now is, yet hastily, and as it were in passing, he strains toward the light of heavenly wisdom.

*Because he was to pass that way. ((ISID.))* In that part where the sycomore was, or where he was to believe, etc., *as far as* he stood out as in the fruitful height of a work.

*And when he was come.* Through the heralds of his word sent before, in whom Jesus was and was speaking, he came to the people of the nations, which, already lifted on high by faith in his passion, burns to acknowledge his divinity also; looking up he sees, for he chose him who through faith had been raised from earthly things and who was choosing him, and loves him who loves him. *Come down.* That he is bidden to come down from the sycomore, and so to make ready a lodging in his house, this is what the Apostle says: *Although we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him not. For if he died of weakness, yet now he lives by the power of God ((II Cor. V, XIII))* . *To abide.* The Lord once abode in the house of the chief of the Pharisees, that is, he was teaching in the synagogue of the Jews.

*They murmured.* It is manifest that the Jews always hated, or did not understand, the salvation of the Gentiles. Whence also it is said against Peter: *Why didst thou go in to the Gentiles that have uncircumcision ((Act. IX))* ?

*But standing,* etc. While others were calumniating him as a sinful man, Zacchaeus himself also standing, that is, persisting in that truth of faith which he had begun, proves that he was not only converted from a sinner, but had even lived among the innocent, since he lived innocently even before his conversion, and he who before his conversion could give the half, after his conversion can give the whole also. *If I have taken anything,* etc. The first thing is to restore according to the law, then to give out to the poor what remains. This fruit of life the publican gathers from the sycomore through wise folly, in that he restores what he has seized, leaves what is near, despises things visible, and longs to follow the footsteps of him whom he does not yet see.

*He is a son.* Not by flesh, but by faith, because as Abraham at God's command forsook his country for the hope of a future inheritance, so also this man, who acquires by hope a treasure in the heavens.

*He came,* etc. Even to those murmuring he does not disdain to expound his mysteries: that he himself came upon earth chiefly for the sake of the repentance of sinners, which is to be looked upon, where also he calls himself the Son of man, that he may intimate to us the dispensation of his mercy.

echoes.text: Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The epistolary salutation 'Grace to you and peace' draws on the Aaronic blessing, where the LORD's gracious face and the gift of peace (shalom) are pronounced over Israel. Paul reworks the priestly benediction into a christological greeting that names both Father and Lord Jesus as its source. The link is formulaic and contested as a deliberate allusion.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Paul's 'boast about you in the assemblies of God' inverts Jeremiah's prohibition against boasting in wisdom, might, or wealth, redirecting glorying toward what God has wrought in the believers' faith. The motif of legitimate versus illegitimate boasting is a Pauline staple rooted in this oracle. Faint and contested here, since the object of boasting differs.

echoes.text: I saw, and the same horn made war with the saints, and prevailed against them; until the ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High, and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom. Thus he said, The fourth animal shall be a fourth kingdom on earth, which shall be diverse from all the kingdoms, and shall devour the whole earth, and shall tread it down, and break it in pieces. As for the ten horns, out of this […]
echoes.note: The endurance of the assembly under 'persecutions and afflictions' resonates with Daniel's vision of the little horn making war on and wearing out the holy ones before their vindication. The apocalyptic pattern of saints suffering prior to the kingdom undergirds the whole chapter. The verbal contact is thematic rather than lexical.

echoes.text: “If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it, or sells it; he shall pay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.
echoes.note: Zacchaeus pledges to restore fourfold what he has wrongfully exacted, matching the Torah's penalty of four sheep for a stolen sheep. Luke's specific multiplier 'four times' aligns precisely with the lower of the Exodus restitution scales, signaling Zacchaeus's voluntary embrace of legal restitution beyond mere repayment. High volume and coherence with the conversion-as-restoration theme.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel: ‘When a man or woman commits any sin that men commit, so as to trespass against Yahweh, and that soul is guilty; then he shall confess his sin which he has done, and he shall make restitution for his guilt in full, and add to it the fifth part of it, and give it to him in respect of whom he has been guilty.
echoes.note: Numbers prescribes that one who wrongs another must confess, restore the principal in full, and add a fifth. Zacchaeus's confession plus voluntary restitution enacts this penitential statute, even exceeding it in the fourfold portion. The coherence of confession-and-restoration makes this a strong background for the verse's logic of repentance.

echoes.text: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but the fat and the strong I will destroy; I will feed them in justice.
echoes.note: The Son of Man's mission to 'seek and to save that which was lost' echoes Ezekiel's promise that God himself will seek the lost sheep and bind up the strayed, in contrast to the false shepherds. Luke applies the divine shepherd-search directly to Jesus, with the rare verb pairing seek/lost matching the prophetic oracle. High volume and thematic coherence with Luke's lost-and-found motif.

echoes.text: He shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity!”
echoes.note: Nathan's parable has David decree the rich thief must restore the lamb fourfold, the same multiplier Zacchaeus invokes. The shared fourfold figure tied to a wealthy man's exploitation of the poor gives a narrative echo, though it derives the number from the Exodus statute David applies. Medium confidence as the link is mediated through the legal background.

echoes.text: therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between sheep and sheep.
echoes.note: Ezekiel adds that God will 'save' his flock so they shall no more be a prey, reinforcing the seek-and-save pairing of v. 10. The combination of seeking the lost and saving the flock in one oracle undergirds Luke's compressed mission statement. Medium because v. 16 carries the primary verbal weight.

echoes.text: Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations. I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make nations of you. Kings will come out of you. I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.
echoes.note: Jesus declares Zacchaeus 'a son of Abraham,' invoking the Abrahamic covenant and its promise of inclusion. The phrase asserts that the despised tax collector belongs to the covenant family, an echo of God's covenant with Abraham and his offspring. Medium volume; the title is idiomatic but covenantally loaded in Luke.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that the Lord will set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant that is left of his people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
echoes.note: The gathering of the scattered/lost of Israel as a restoration motif faintly underlies 'came to seek and to save that which was lost.' The remnant-gathering theme coheres with Luke's salvation-to-this-house, but the verbal contact is slight. Low confidence; Ezekiel 34 is the stronger source.

echoes.text: “In that day,” says Yahweh, “I will assemble that which is lame, and I will gather that which is driven away, and that which I have afflicted;
echoes.note: Micah's promise to gather 'her that is driven out' and 'the lost' (LXX) supplies another prophetic seeking-the-lost background for v. 10. The image of God assembling the strayed remnant coheres with Jesus's mission statement but is verbally faint beside Ezekiel. Low confidence, marked contested.

notes.text: Of Sodom — So called for their resemblance of them in wickedness. The law - The message which I am now to deliver to you from God, your great lawgiver. 11. To me - Who am a spirit, and therefore cannot be satisfied with such carnal oblations, but expect to have your hearts and lives, as well as your bodies and sacrifices, presented unto me. Blood - He mentions the fat and blood, because these were in a peculiar manner reserved for God, to intimate that even the best of their sacrifices were rejected by him.

To appear — Upon the three solemn feasts, or upon other occasions. Who required - The thing I commanded, was not only, nor chiefly, that you should offer external sacrifices, but that you should do it with true repentance, with faith in my promises, and sincere resolutions of devoting yourselves to my service.
The solemn meeting — The most solemn day of each of the three feasts, which was the last day.
Blood — You are guilty of murder, and oppression.
Wash — Cleanse your hearts and hands.
Learn — Begin to live soberly, righteously, and godly. Judgment - Shew your religion to God, by practicing justice to men. Judge - Defend and deliver them.

glossa.text: *Hear the word.* ((ID.)) The remnant being saved, etc., *as far as* and now he is discerned by the mind, when he is believed to be invisible.

*I am full.* ((ID.)) As if he should say: Do you think that I have need of these things, or take delight in them? But I am full, that is, I have need of nothing. *For mine is the earth and the fulness thereof.* Or, I am full, that is, affected with weariness, because you do not offer rightly.

*The holocausts of rams,* etc., as far as: *To judge for the fatherless,* etc. He rejects the sacrifices of the Jews, he commends the obedience of the Gospel: *The holocausts of rams,* etc. He points to the last destruction of the temple, which endures for ever. For after the Babylonian captivity the temple was built by Zorobabel, and sacrifice was offered in it for a long time.

((ID.)) *The holocausts of rams.* It can also be taken of those who, while they despise the precepts of God, wish to appease him by a multitude of sacrifices, and to buy themselves licence to sin. Or of those who offer robbery and avarice upon the altar, and bestow them on the poor.

*I would not.* Using the past tense, he shows that he never loved the sacrifices of the Jews, but bore with them for a time on account of what they signified; and that, the true sacrifice being fulfilled, he reckoned them as nothing.

*When you came.* ((ID.)) God did not seek these sacrifices as though he were in need; but that they might not sacrifice to demons, and that through carnal and typical things they might come more easily to the spiritual and true sacrifice.

*Who required?* Let the Ebionites hear this, who after the passion of Christ think that the law is to be kept: let their fellows hear this, who decree that it is to be kept only by the Israelite race.

*The new moon,* etc, The feast of the new moon, which they used to celebrate at the beginning of the months: *Neos,* new, *mene,* moon; whence: *Blow up the trumpet to the Lord on the new moon ((Psal. LXXX))*.

*Your assemblies are wicked,* etc. ((ID.)) Because they do not offer spiritual victims; whence: *A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit ((Psalm. L))*.

*My soul hath hated.* ((ID.)) Ανθρωποσπαθῶς. Not that he has a soul, but he speaks after our manner; as if to say, I have utterly hated.

*I have labored,* etc. ((HIER.)) Symmachus. *I have failed in pitying,* etc., *as far as* but thou art saved by my help alone.
*For your hands are full of blood,* etc. ((ID.)) Of the Prophets, and at last of their Lord, etc., *as far as* they keep watch in prayer by day and by night.

*Be washed,* etc. As if he should say: This I have hated: the truth of the Gospel pleases me: *Be washed,* in the blood of Christ, in the water of baptism. *Be clean,* abiding in innocence of life. For baptism alone avails unto the remission of sin, whence: *Unless a man be born again ((Joan. III))*, etc. And elsewhere: *Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father,* etc.

((HIER., ubi supra )). The chief order, etc., *as far as* but also in the sight of God, from whom nothing can be hidden.

*Cease to do perversely.* ((ID.)) It sounds that saying of the Gospel, etc., *as far as* whom they follow in the Apocalypse who shine with the whiteness of virginity.

*Learn to do well.* ((ID.)) Not trusting in nature, etc., *as far as* the thresholds of masters must be worn away.

*Seek judgment,* etc. ((ID.)) To the victims of the Jews the commandments of the Gospel succeed. Provision is made for orphans and widows, so that the martyrs, secure concerning their wives and children, may go forth to their battles.

*As scarlet,* etc. ((ID.)) The same thing is the scarlet grain and the scarlet, and the little worm, namely a great sin, and murder and adultery, etc. But what is signified by snow, this is signified by wool: the purging, that is, and the washing away of sins.

*As snow.* Because they shall be cold against the incitements of vices: *And as wool,* because they are clothed against the cold of faithlessness.

*White wool,* etc. ((ID.)) Of which the garment of Christ is made.

notes.text: Imputeth — Whom God doth not charge with the guilt of his sins, but graciously pardons and accepts him in Christ. No guile - Who freely confesses all his sins, and turns from sin to God with all his heart.

Silence — From a full and open confession of my sins. Old - My spirit failed, and the strength of my body decayed. Roaring - Because of the continual horrors of my conscience, and sense of God's wrath.
Hand — Thy afflicting hand. My moisture - Was dried up.
The iniquity — The guilt of my sin.

For this — Upon the encouragement of my example. Found - In an acceptable and seasonable time, while God continues to offer grace and mercy. Waters - In the time of great calamities. Not come - So as to overwhelm him.

glossa.text: *Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven,* etc. ((AUG.)) Not those in whom he finds no sin, but those to whom he forgives it. *Iniquities.* He means the tinder of sin, namely concupiscence, etc., *as far as* but that sin may be no more. ((HIERON.)) Iniquities, before faith and baptism: sin, after faith and baptism.

*Blessed is the man.* ((HIERON.)) To whom God forgives, for not of himself. He covers it, that it be not revealed in the judgment; and so it will not be imputed unto punishment. There is no guile in him that accuses himself: he holds in the heart what he confesses here with the mouth.

*Blessed:* because formerly, not confessing to God, I came into sin, while I cried out, if I did any good.

*I was silent.* ((AUG.)) He who will not confess his sins labours without cause in the defence of sins: and since in this he also boasts of his merits, his strength fails the more. ((CASS.)) *Blessed is he to whom he hath not imputed.* To some, who have grievous sins, God imputes them; to others he does not impute them, through mercy, even though they have some — namely to those who do not proclaim themselves just when they are evil, but acknowledging themselves make satisfaction. This I now profess, but formerly: *Because I was silent,* etc. ((AUG.)) Or, *I was silent,* as to sin with my voice, *while I cried out all the day:* while the penalty of sin, or an inward blinding, showed me a sinner, or while my evil life cried out, though I was silent, whether I had done any good.

*While I cried out all the day,* etc. Although a man be not conscious to himself of anything, yet he is not just: for who understands his offences? Whence: *There is a just man that perisheth in his own justice.* And the Apostle: *I am conscious to myself of nothing,* etc.
*The thorn is fastened in.* ((CASS.)) *The thorn,* which lifts up the whole body, that is, pride. ((AUG.)) Likewise *misery,* etc., *as far as: in the hands of a drunken man.*
*My sin.* Diapsalma. Confession, whence pardon, as above the growing old from governance. *I have made known.* ((CASS.)) For *I said* before, etc., *as far as* and God hears.

*For this shall he pray.* ((ID.)) Diapsalma. Commending repentance, he says it is common to all the saints; which sundry sects reject, against whom he flees for refuge to God. ((AUG.)) *For this.* Therefore every saint prays, because thou hast forgiven, otherwise he would not be a saint. *In the time,* etc. It is the time of grace, the law, pressing and convicting the guilty, compelled them to cry out, grace heals. *But yet in the flood,* etc. ((AUG.)) Although the saint pray, etc., *as far as* the saint will pray, saying: *Thou art a refuge. To him.* That is, to God, for he changes the person, as often. They do not draw near who say that fate makes them sin, or fortune, which rules all things, or the people of darkness, which rebels against God.

V, XIII))* . *To abide.* The Lord once abode in the house of the chief of the Pharisees, that is, he was teaching in the synagogue of the Jews.

Paul reworks the priestly benediction into a christological greeting that names both Father and Lord Jesus as its source. The link is formulaic and contested as a deliberate allusion.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: Paul's 'boast about you in the assemblies of God' inverts Jeremiah's prohibition against boasting in wisdom, might, or wealth, redirecting glorying toward what God has wrought in the believers' faith. The motif of legitimate versus illegitimate boasting is a Pauline staple rooted in this oracle. Faint and contested here, since the object of boasting differs.

echoes.text: I saw, and the same horn made war with the saints, and prevailed against them; until the ancient of days came, and judgment was given to the saints of the Most High, and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom. Thus he said, The fourth animal shall be a fourth kingdom on earth, which shall be diverse from all the kingdoms, and shall devour the whole earth, and shall tread it down, and break it in pieces. As for the ten horns, out of this […]
echoes.note: The endurance of the assembly under 'persecutions and afflictions' resonates with Daniel's vision of the little horn making war on and wearing out the holy ones before their vindication. The apocalyptic pattern of saints suffering prior to the kingdom undergirds the whole chapter. The verbal contact is thematic rather than lexical.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it, or sells it; he shall pay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.
echoes.note: Zacchaeus pledges to restore fourfold what he has wrongfully exacted, matching the Torah's penalty of four sheep for a stolen sheep. Luke's specific multiplier 'four times' aligns precisely with the lower of the Exodus restitution scales, signaling Zacchaeus's voluntary embrace of legal restitution beyond mere repayment. High volume and coherence with the conversion-as-restoration theme.

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel: ‘When a man or woman commits any sin that men commit, so as to trespass against Yahweh, and that soul is guilty; then he shall confess his sin which he has done, and he shall make restitution for his guilt in full, and add to it the fifth part of it, and give it to him in respect of whom he has been guilty.
echoes.note: Numbers prescribes that one who wrongs another must confess, restore the principal in full, and add a fifth. Zacchaeus's confession plus voluntary restitution enacts this penitential statute, even exceeding it in the fourfold portion. The coherence of confession-and-restoration makes this a strong background for the verse's logic of repentance.

echoes.text: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but the fat and the strong I will destroy; I will feed them in justice.
echoes.note: The Son of Man's mission to 'seek and to save that which was lost' echoes Ezekiel's promise that God himself will seek the lost sheep and bind up the strayed, in contrast to the false shepherds. Luke applies the divine shepherd-search directly to Jesus, with the rare verb pairing seek/lost matching the prophetic oracle. High volume and thematic coherence with Luke's lost-and-found motif.

echoes.text: He shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity!”
echoes.note: Nathan's parable has David decree the rich thief must restore the lamb fourfold, the same multiplier Zacchaeus invokes. The shared fourfold figure tied to a wealthy man's exploitation of the poor gives a narrative echo, though it derives the number from the Exodus statute David applies. Medium confidence as the link is mediated through the legal background.

echoes.text: therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between sheep and sheep.
echoes.note: Ezekiel adds that God will 'save' his flock so they shall no more be a prey, reinforcing the seek-and-save pairing of v. 10. The combination of seeking the lost and saving the flock in one oracle undergirds Luke's compressed mission statement. Medium because v. 16 carries the primary verbal weight.

echoes.text: Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations. I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make nations of you. Kings will come out of you. I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you.
echoes.note: Jesus declares Zacchaeus 'a son of Abraham,' invoking the Abrahamic covenant and its promise of inclusion. The phrase asserts that the despised tax collector belongs to the covenant family, an echo of God's covenant with Abraham and his offspring. Medium volume; the title is idiomatic but covenantally loaded in Luke.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day that the Lord will set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant that is left of his people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
echoes.note: The gathering of the scattered/lost of Israel as a restoration motif faintly underlies 'came to seek and to save that which was lost.' The remnant-gathering theme coheres with Luke's salvation-to-this-house, but the verbal contact is slight. Low confidence; Ezekiel 34 is the stronger source.

echoes.text: “In that day,” says Yahweh, “I will assemble that which is lame, and I will gather that which is driven away, and that which I have afflicted;
echoes.note: Micah's promise to gather 'her that is driven out' and 'the lost' (LXX) supplies another prophetic seeking-the-lost background for v. 10. The image of God assembling the strayed remnant coheres with Jesus's mission statement but is verbally faint beside Ezekiel. Low confidence, marked contested.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Happy are those whose transgression is forgiven.
Today salvation has come to this house.
Zacchaeus, hurry down; I must stay at your house today.
Today salvation has come to this house.
Wash, make clean; learn to do good, seek justice.
Come, let us worship. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: A small, despised man climbs a tree just to see, and Jesus stops and calls him by name.
Today salvation has come to this house.
Come down, I must stay with you — and grace walks straight into a house everyone avoided.
Today salvation has come to this house.
The change is real: half to the poor, fourfold to the cheated, a life turned right-side up.
Today salvation has come to this house.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost — which is to say, came for us.
Today salvation has come to this house!
